questions.question: What is the difference between mutable and immutable objects in Python?
questions.title: Mutable vs Immutable Objects in Python
questions.direct_answer: A mutable object can be changed in place, while an immutable object's value cannot change after creation. Assignment binds a name to an object, so aliases to a mutable object observe the same updates.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand object identity, aliasing, in-place changes, and the effect of passing collections to functions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing the variable as mutable instead of the object, or assuming an immutable tuple cannot contain a mutable object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that assignment does not copy an object and show how two names can refer to the same list.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Understand what can change, what keeps the same identity, and why an update through one name may be visible through another.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Lists, dictionaries, sets, and bytearrays are mutable; their contents can change in place.
Numbers, strings, bytes, tuples, and frozensets are immutable.
Assignment binds another name to the same object; it does not make a copy.
An operation on an immutable value creates or returns another object instead of changing that value.
A tuple is an immutable container, but an object stored inside it can still be mutable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Mutability is a property of an object, not of the variable name that refers to it. A mutable object can keep the same identity while its contents change; lists, dictionaries, sets, and bytearrays are common examples. An immutable object's value cannot change after creation; numbers, strings, bytes, tuples, and frozensets are common examples.

Assignment binds a name to an existing object and does not copy it. After `alias = original`, both names may reach the same list. Calling `original.append(3)` changes that one list, so the update is also visible through `alias`. This is shared identity, not Python synchronizing two separate values.

With an immutable integer, `count += 1` produces another integer and rebinds `count`; it does not modify the object representing `3`. With a list, `items += [4]` can update the same list in place. The same rule crosses a function call: appending to a received list affects the caller's object, while adding to a received integer only changes the function's local binding unless the new value is returned.

Immutability is not always deep. A tuple cannot replace one of its element references, but a list stored inside that tuple can still be changed. That tuple is also not hashable because one of its elements is unhashable. Mutable collections suit state that should evolve; immutable values suit stable facts and dictionary keys when every contained value is hashable.

With a list, `items += [4]` can update the same list in place. support.title: A list mutates while an integer is rebound
support.code:
def add_tag(tags):
    tags.append("python")

def increment(number):
    number += 1
    return number

skills = ["sql"]
alias = skills
add_tag(skills)

level = 1
new_level = increment(level)
print(skills, alias)
print(level, new_level)
support.caption: The two list names show the same change; `level` remains `1` while the returned value is `2`.

Mutable collections suit state that should evolve; immutable values suit stable facts and dictionary keys when every contained value is hashable.

sections.title: Identity, type, and value
sections.content:
Every Python object has an identity, a type, and a value. Identity stays with the object for its lifetime. The type decides which operations are available and whether the value can change.

A list can keep its identity while its elements change. A string cannot change its characters; methods such as `upper()` return another string. This is why `id(values)` can stay the same after `values.append(3)`, while a name may refer to a different string after `text = text.upper()`.

Names do not contain objects. They refer to objects. That reference model explains most surprises involving mutation, function arguments, and shared state.

sections.title: Common built-in objects
sections.content:
| Object type | Mutable? | Typical change | Important boundary |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `list` | Yes | `items.append(x)` | Aliases see the appended item |
| `dict` | Yes | `record[key] = value` | Keys must be hashable |
| `set` | Yes | `seen.add(x)` | Elements must be hashable |
| `str` / numbers | No | Operation returns another value | Do not rely on reused identities |
| `tuple` | No as a container | Element references cannot be replaced | A referenced list can still mutate |
| `frozenset` | No | Set operation returns another frozenset | Can be a key when its elements are hashable |

sections.title: Why an alias sees a mutation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[name: original] --> L["list object [1, 2]"]
  B[name: alias] --> L
  M["original.append(3)"] --> L2["same list object [1, 2, 3]"]
  L --> L2
```

Both names reach one list. The append changes that list; it does not create an independent value for `original`.

sections.title: Observe mutation and rebinding
sections.content:
```python
def add_tag(tags):
    tags.append("python")  # changes the caller's list

def increment(number):
    number += 1              # rebinds only this local name
    return number

skills = ["sql"]
alias = skills
add_tag(skills)

level = 1
new_level = increment(level)

print(skills, alias)    # ['sql', 'python'] ['sql', 'python']
print(level, new_level) # 1 2
```

The first output demonstrates shared mutation. The second shows that changing an immutable integer produces a new result.

sections.title: Check the boundary
sections.content: Consider `record = ([1, 2], "ready")`. The tuple cannot replace either element, but `record[0].append(3)` is valid because the first element refers to a mutable list. The tuple itself remains an immutable container.

questions.question: When should you use a list, tuple, set, or dictionary in Python?
questions.title: Choosing Python's Core Collection Type
questions.direct_answer: Use a list for an ordered, changeable sequence; a tuple for a fixed sequence; a set for unique values and membership tests; and a dictionary for key-to-value lookup.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you choose a collection from the data relationship rather than from habit.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a list for every problem, then manually enforcing uniqueness or repeatedly scanning for keyed data.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose from ordering, duplication, lookup, and mutation requirements, then name the hashability boundary.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Turn the shape of the data into a collection choice: sequence, fixed record, unique membership, or key-to-value mapping.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Choose `list` when order matters and items may be added, removed, or replaced.
Choose `tuple` for a fixed-position group or a sequence that should not be structurally changed.
Choose `set` for uniqueness, set operations, and fast average membership checks.
Choose `dict` when each value is found or updated through a meaningful key.
Set elements and dictionary keys must be hashable; a tuple is hashable only when all its elements are hashable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Use a list for an ordered sequence whose contents may grow, shrink, or be replaced. A task queue shown in arrival order is a simple example. Lists allow duplicates, support indexing, and make operations such as `tasks.append(new_task)` explicit. They are a poor substitute for a keyed index or for uniqueness rules that must be enforced manually.

Use a tuple when positions form a fixed group, such as `(latitude, longitude)`, and the outer structure should not be edited. A tuple may be a dictionary key when every element is hashable. It does not freeze objects stored inside it, so a tuple containing a list is neither deeply immutable nor hashable.

Use a set when the important question is whether a value is present, when duplicates should disappear, or when union, intersection, and difference describe the problem. `required_skills <= candidate_skills` directly tests whether every required skill is present. Do not choose a set when duplicate counts or positional order carry meaning, and do not depend on its iteration order.

Use a dictionary when a meaningful key identifies each value, as in `users_by_id[user_id]`. Keys are unique and hashable, while values may be any objects. Dictionaries preserve insertion order in current Python, but their main signal is the key-to-value relationship and direct average-case lookup rather than a repeated scan through a list.

One order model can use several collection types without conflict: a list keeps line-item order, each tuple holds a fixed `(sku, quantity)` pair, a set records unique promotion codes, and a dictionary finds product names by SKU. The best type is the narrowest one that preserves the ordering, duplicate, mutation, and lookup rules the application actually needs.

beats.spokenText: Use a list for an ordered sequence whose contents may grow, shrink, or be replaced. A task queue shown in arrival order is a simple example. Lists allow duplicates, support indexing, and make operations such as `tasks.append(new_task)` explicit. They are a poor substitute for a keyed index or for uniqueness rules that must be enforced manually.

support.title: Four collections in one small order
support.caption: Each type records a different rule instead of forcing every relationship into a list.

beats.recallRule: Use list for ordered work, tuple for fixed positions, set for unique membership, and dict for keyed lookup.

sections.title: Choosing a type from the data relationship
sections.content:
A collection type is part of the model, not merely storage syntax. `['draft', 'sent', 'sent']` says order and repetition matter. `{'draft', 'sent'}` says only membership and uniqueness matter. `{'A17': 'sent'}` says a stable key identifies a value.

Lists and tuples are sequences, so iteration follows position. Sets describe membership and mathematical relationships; code should not depend on a set's iteration order. Dictionaries connect keys to values and, in current Python, iterate in insertion order.

Hash-based collections need stable hashes. Mutable containers such as lists and dictionaries cannot be set elements or dictionary keys because their changing value would break lookup.

sections.title: A practical collection decision
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[What relationship matters?] --> B{Key maps to value?}
  B -- Yes --> D[dict]
  B -- No --> C{Uniqueness or set operations?}
  C -- Yes --> S[set]
  C -- No --> F{Fixed structure?}
  F -- Yes --> T[tuple]
  F -- No --> L[list]
```

This is a starting point. Verify ordering, duplicate, mutation, and hashability requirements before deciding.

sections.title: Compare the guarantees
sections.content:
| Type | Ordered iteration | Duplicates | Mutable container | Best signal |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `list` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Ordered working sequence |
| `tuple` | Yes | Yes | No | Fixed-position sequence |
| `set` | Do not rely on it | No | Yes | Unique membership |
| `dict` | Insertion order | Keys are unique | Yes | Key-to-value mapping |

sections.title: Model one order with four relationships
sections.content:
```python
line_items = [("A17", 2), ("B04", 1)]       # ordered, fixed pairs
applied_codes = {"WELCOME", "FREESHIP"}        # unique membership
products = {"A17": "Keyboard", "B04": "Mouse"} # lookup by SKU

for sku, quantity in line_items:
    print(quantity, products[sku])

print("FREESHIP" in applied_codes)
```

The code does not need comments explaining duplicate rules or lookup intent because the selected types already express much of that design.

sections.title: One-minute check
sections.content: Choose a type for each case: browser history → `list`; RGB colour → `tuple`; unique visitors → `set`; employee by ID → `dict`. If the answer changes, name the requirement that changed it.

followup_questions: Why must dictionary keys and set elements be hashable?
When is a tuple still not hashable?
How would you preserve both uniqueness and first-seen order?

questions.question: Why are mutable default arguments dangerous in Python?
questions.title: Mutable Default Arguments in Python
questions.direct_answer: A default argument is evaluated once when the function is defined, not on every call. If that default is a mutable object, later calls reuse its changed state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when defaults are created and how state can leak across function calls.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `[]`, `{}`, or `set()` as a default when each call is supposed to receive fresh state.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish an accidental shared default from an intentional cache, and use a `None` sentinel for fresh state.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Connect function definition time to repeated calls and understand why the usual `None` sentinel creates independent state.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Python evaluates default expressions when the `def` statement runs.
The same default object is reused whenever the caller omits that argument.
Mutating a default list, dictionary, or set makes its state visible to later calls.
Use `None` as a sentinel and create the collection inside the function when fresh state is required.
Shared defaults can be intentional for caching, but that behavior should be explicit and documented.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python evaluates default argument expressions when the `def` statement runs. The resulting objects are stored with the function and reused whenever a later call omits those arguments. A default list therefore lives with the function rather than belonging to one call, which is the lifetime mismatch behind this bug.

In `def add_item(item, basket=[])`, the expression `basket.append(item)` mutates the stored default. Calling `add_item("book")` and then `add_item("pen")` makes the second result contain both items. The problem is not that lists are invalid arguments; it is that callers expecting fresh state silently share one object.

When every omitted argument needs a new collection, use `None` as a sentinel and create the list inside the function. Check `basket is None`, not `if not basket`, because an explicitly supplied empty list is a valid caller-owned object and should not be replaced. A supplied list is still mutated intentionally by this version.

A mutable default can deliberately act as a cache or accumulator, but that shared lifetime should be obvious and documented. In application code, an explicitly named cache object, closure, or class usually communicates the ownership better than hidden state in a signature. Keep stable immutable defaults in the signature and create per-call mutable state inside the body.

beats.cue: Place default evaluation at function definition time
beats.spokenText: Python evaluates default argument expressions when the `def` statement runs. The resulting objects are stored with the function and reused whenever a later call omits those arguments. A default list therefore lives with the function rather than belonging to one call, which is the lifetime mismatch behind this bug.

items.label: First omitted argument

items.label: Second omitted argument

Calling `add_item("book")` and then `add_item("pen")` makes the second result contain both items. The problem is not that lists are invalid arguments; it is that callers expecting fresh state silently share one object.

Check `basket is None`, not `if not basket`, because an explicitly supplied empty list is a valid caller-owned object and should not be replaced. A supplied list is still mutated intentionally by this version.

support.title: Definition-time default and call-time list
support.code:
def unsafe_add(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

def safe_add(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(unsafe_add("book"))
print(unsafe_add("pen"))
print(safe_add("book"))
print(safe_add("pen"))
support.caption: The unsafe calls accumulate state; the safe omitted arguments produce independent lists.

beats.cue: Separate deliberate shared state from accidental state
beats.spokenText: A mutable default can deliberately act as a cache or accumulator, but that shared lifetime should be obvious and documented. In application code, an explicitly named cache object, closure, or class usually communicates the ownership better than hidden state in a signature. Keep stable immutable defaults in the signature and create per-call mutable state inside the body.
beats.recallRule: Default expressions run once at definition time; create mutable per-call values inside the function body.

sections.title: Definition time versus call time
sections.content:
A `def` statement is executable. When Python reaches it, Python creates the function object and evaluates the default expressions. Calling the function later binds omitted parameters to those stored default objects.

The bug is therefore about lifetime: the list lives as long as the function, not as long as one call. Mutating it is observable state. A `None` sentinel delays creation of the real list until call time, which gives each omitted argument a fresh object.

sections.title: One object across three moments
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["Definition: create default list []"] --> C1["Call 1: append 'book'"]
  C1 --> S1["stored default: ['book']"]
  S1 --> C2["Call 2: append 'pen'"]
  C2 --> S2["stored default: ['book', 'pen']"]
```

No new default list is created between the two calls.

sections.title: See the bug and the safe form
sections.content:
```python
def unsafe_add(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

def safe_add(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(unsafe_add("book")) # ['book']
print(unsafe_add("pen"))  # ['book', 'pen']
print(safe_add("book"))   # ['book']
print(safe_add("pen"))    # ['pen']
```

An explicitly supplied list is still mutated by `safe_add`; the sentinel only controls what happens when the argument is omitted.

sections.title: Choose the default from the required lifetime
sections.content:
| Requirement | Signature | Result |
|---|---|---|
| No value has a clear meaning | `value=None` | Stable singleton default |
| Fresh collection per call | `items=None`, then create `[]` | Calls are isolated |
| Caller supplies a collection | `items=None` or required `items` | Caller controls ownership |
| Shared cache by design | Explicit cache object or documented default | Shared lifetime is visible |

followup_questions: When are function default expressions evaluated?
Why should the sentinel check use `is None` instead of `if not items`?
How can a caller intentionally pass and reuse its own list?

questions.question: What is the difference between assignment, a shallow copy, and a deep copy in Python?
questions.title: Assignment vs Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
questions.direct_answer: Assignment creates another reference to the same object. A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares nested objects; a deep copy recursively copies nested objects too.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about nested references and choose the minimum isolation the program needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming `list.copy()` isolates lists nested inside the copied list.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace both the outer and inner identities and note that deep copy can be expensive or unsuitable for some object graphs.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Follow references at every nesting level and choose copying from the required ownership boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `alias = original` binds two names to the same object and copies nothing.
A shallow copy creates a new outer object but reuses references to nested objects.
A deep copy recursively copies nested objects while using memoization to handle repeated references and cycles.
Use a shallow copy when only the outer container will change; use deep copy only when nested state must be isolated.
Prefer constructing the exact new value you need when a full deep copy would copy too much.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Assignment creates no copy. After `alias = original`, both names refer to the same outer object and therefore reach the same nested objects too. Any in-place change made through either name is visible through the other. This is appropriate only when both parts of the program are meant to share one state.

A shallow copy creates a new outer container and places references to the original nested objects inside it. For a list, `original.copy()`, `list(original)`, slicing, and `copy.copy(original)` are shallow operations. Appending an outer element affects only the copy, but editing `shallow[0]` may still change data seen by `original[0]`.

`copy.deepcopy(original)` walks the object graph and recursively copies nested content. It keeps a memo of objects already copied, which preserves repeated references consistently and prevents infinite recursion on cycles. The result can edit copied nested lists or dictionaries without changing their originals, unless a type defines special copying behaviour or remains shared.

The important test is not only whether the outer lists differ, but whether their nested elements differ. In the example, `shallow.append(...)` changes only the shallow outer list, `shallow[0].append(...)` reaches a nested list shared with the original, and an edit inside `deep` stays inside the copied graph.

Use a shallow copy when only outer membership or order will change. Consider deep copy when nested mutable state must be independent, but remember that it costs more work and memory and may be wrong for files, connections, caches, or identity-sensitive objects. A targeted rebuild is often clearer because it copies exactly the fields whose ownership must change.

beats.spokenText: Assignment creates no copy. After `alias = original`, both names refer to the same outer object and therefore reach the same nested objects too. Any in-place change made through either name is visible through the other. This is appropriate only when both parts of the program are meant to share one state.

beats.cue: Demonstrate the outer and nested identity boundary
beats.spokenText: The important test is not only whether the outer lists differ, but whether their nested elements differ. In the example, `shallow.append(...)` changes only the shallow outer list, `shallow[0].append(...)` reaches a nested list shared with the original, and an edit inside `deep` stays inside the copied graph.

support.title: Trace one outer change and two nested changes
support.code:
from copy import deepcopy

original = [["Ada"], ["Linus"]]
alias = original
shallow = original.copy()
deep = deepcopy(original)

shallow.append(["Grace"])
shallow[0].append("Lovelace")
deep[1].append("Torvalds")

print(alias is original)
print(original)
print(shallow)
print(deep)
support.caption: The shallow outer list differs, but its first nested list is still shared with `original`.

beats.cue: Choose the smallest ownership boundary that works
beats.spokenText: Use a shallow copy when only outer membership or order will change. Consider deep copy when nested mutable state must be independent, but remember that it costs more work and memory and may be wrong for files, connections, caches, or identity-sensitive objects. A targeted rebuild is often clearer because it copies exactly the fields whose ownership must change.
beats.recallRule: Assignment shares everything, shallow copy separates the outer object, and deep copy follows nested references.

sections.title: Copying is a graph problem
sections.content:
A nested container is a graph of references. The outer list refers to inner dictionaries or lists, and those objects may refer to more objects. The word “copy” is incomplete until the required depth is clear.

Assignment adds a name to the same graph. Shallow copy duplicates only the first node and keeps its outgoing references. Deep copy walks the graph, creates copies, and records objects it has already copied so that repeated references and recursive structures are handled consistently.

Often a targeted reconstruction is clearer than `deepcopy`: for example, `{**user, "address": {**user["address"]}}` documents exactly which nested dictionary becomes independent.

sections.title: Which objects are shared?
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[original outer list] --> N[nested list]
  A[assignment alias] --> O
  S[shallow-copy outer list] --> N
  D[deep-copy outer list] --> N2[copied nested list]
```

Assignment shares the outer and inner objects. Shallow copy separates only the outer object. Deep copy separates the nested mutable object as well.

sections.title: Compare the three operations
sections.content:
| Operation | New outer object? | Nested objects shared? | Typical use |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Assignment | No | Yes | Intentional alias to one state |
| Shallow copy | Yes | Yes | Change outer membership or order |
| Deep copy | Yes | Usually no | Independent nested edits |
| Targeted rebuild | Yes where selected | By explicit choice | Precise ownership with less copying |

sections.title: Trace outer and nested mutations
sections.content:
```python
from copy import deepcopy

original = [["Ada"], ["Linus"]]
alias = original
shallow = original.copy()
deep = deepcopy(original)

shallow.append(["Grace"]) # only shallow's outer list changes
shallow[0].append("Lovelace") # shared nested list changes
deep[1].append("Torvalds")   # copied nested list changes

print(original) # [['Ada', 'Lovelace'], ['Linus']]
print(alias)    # same object as original
print(shallow)  # plus ['Grace']; nested first list is shared
print(deep)     # [['Ada'], ['Linus', 'Torvalds']]
```

sections.title: Pick the required isolation
sections.content: If a report needs only a differently sorted outer list, make a shallow copy. If an editor may change nested address fields without changing the saved user, copy or rebuild the address too. The operation follows the mutation boundary.

questions.question: How do you debug unexpected changes caused by shared mutable objects in Python?
questions.title: Debugging Shared Mutable State in Python
questions.direct_answer: Find the first mutation, then check which names reference that object with `is` or `id()`. Fix the ownership boundary by copying, returning new data, or making mutation explicit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can diagnose an aliasing bug from evidence instead of treating it as random state corruption.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Logging only equal values and missing that two parts of the program own the same mutable object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Locate the first write, draw the reference graph, and choose a clear ownership contract rather than adding copies everywhere.

sections.title: Learning goal
sections.content: Turn an apparently distant state change into a small trace of object identity, aliases, and the first in-place write.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Reproduce the bug with the smallest data structure and one mutation.
Use `a is b` or temporary `id()` output to discover aliases; equality alone is not enough.
Inspect in-place operations such as `append`, `extend`, item assignment, `update`, and `+=` on mutable containers.
Identify who owns the object and whether mutation is part of the function's contract.
Prove the fix with a regression test that checks both the result and the original input.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Reduce the failure to the smallest object and operation that still reproduces the unexpected change. Then move backward from the visible symptom to the first point where the value differs from what was expected. Later incorrect values are usually consequences; the first in-place write is the useful debugging target.

Compare identity as well as value. `a == b` says two objects currently hold equal values, while `a is b` says both names refer to one object. Temporary `id()` output can help pair references during debugging, but application logic should not depend on that numeric ID. Draw the names and the objects they reach when nesting is involved.

Between the last good state and the first bad state, inspect calls such as `append`, `extend`, `sort`, `dict.update`, `set.add`, item assignment, deletion, and mutable `+=`. A helper can change an object owned by its caller even when it returns nothing. The write may be far from the code that later notices it.

A shallow copy can make the outer container look independent while its nested records remain shared. After `draft = saved.copy()`, `draft is saved` is false, but `draft[0] is saved[0]` can be true. Building the exact public record avoids removing a private field from the saved source.

Repair the ownership boundary rather than adding copies everywhere. A mutating function can make that contract clear in its name and documentation; a non-mutating function can return newly built data; selected nested fields can be copied when only they need isolation. The regression test should assert both the result and whether the original input must remain unchanged.

sections.title: Find the first write, not the last symptom
sections.content:
Shared-state bugs feel non-local because the write and the symptom use different names. The object connects them. Start with a reference graph: which request, cache, model, or helper owns each mutable container? Then mark every operation that can write to it.

Value logs may be misleading because equality only says contents match. Identity answers whether two paths reach one object. Breakpoints, a watch expression, and temporary `id()` pairs can narrow the alias. Once found, write the ownership rule in ordinary language: “This function may update the supplied list” or “The input remains unchanged.”

The right repair makes that sentence true. It is usually more precise than copying at an arbitrary layer.

sections.title: A focused debugging path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R[Reproduce one unexpected change] --> F[Find the first bad state]
  F --> I{Same object? check `is`}
  I -- Yes --> W[Locate the in-place write]
  I -- No --> C[Check conversion or reassignment]
  W --> O[Define ownership contract]
  O --> X[Copy precisely, return new data, or document mutation]
  X --> T[Test result and original input]
```

sections.title: Expose a nested alias and fix it
sections.content:
```python
def public_view_bad(records):
    result = records.copy()       # outer list only
    for record in result:
        record.pop("secret", None)
    return result

def public_view(records):
    return [
        {key: value for key, value in record.items() if key != "secret"}
        for record in records
    ]

source = [{"name": "Ada", "secret": "token"}]
outer_copy = source.copy()
print(outer_copy[0] is source[0]) # True: nested alias

view = public_view(source)
print(view)   # [{'name': 'Ada'}]
print(source) # original still includes 'secret'
```

The corrected function constructs the public record it needs instead of copying unrelated parts of the graph.

sections.title: Match the repair to the contract
sections.content:
| Required contract | Suitable repair | Test assertion |
|---|---|---|
| Helper owns and mutates input | Make mutation explicit in name/docs | Input has documented new state |
| Caller keeps original unchanged | Build and return new data | Input equals pre-call snapshot |
| Only selected nested fields vary | Copy or rebuild those fields | Shared fields stay safe |
| Whole independent graph required | Consider `deepcopy` | Nested identities differ where required |

sections.title: Trace before changing code
sections.content: For `draft = saved.copy()`, ask two questions separately: Is `draft is saved`? Is `draft['tags'] is saved['tags']`? The first is false and the second may be true. That difference identifies the depth at which ownership is still shared.
